resolution: Elaborated versus verification-only feedback, plus a reason to act on it. Feedback that explains WHY works (S027 item-level explanations of incorrect distractors; S025 immediate feedback on one's own prior reasoning). Feedback that only says right-or-wrong does not (S006, knowledge-of-correct-response only). Two further defeaters: prior knowledge too poor to debug from the feedback at all (S018), and no incentive to revise (S027, formative assessment without credit points).

Guidance, not the cases. The same case material helps when structured and prompted and fails when the learner is left to run it: S018's open, unguided 'diagnose-explain-and-learn' task produced limited learning in advanced students, while the guided similar-case series with variation worked. S025 adds that the model must be reachable, and S026 that prompts are what carry far transfer.

Whether engagement is secured, and whether demand outruns experience. Structured, required practice works (S018, S023, S027). Optional self-directed access does not: S011 reports limited voluntary engagement and restricted uptake from exactly the same virtual patients that worked when embedded in the rotation. Separately, S015 shows practice placing demands beyond the learner's experience (multitasking, pager interruption) produces stress and an abandoned assessment rather than learning.

Same moderator as contradiction 6, at intervention rather than mechanism level: the familiarity window. Self-explanation case solving works on less familiar cases with scope for elaboration (S013, S020, S025, S026) and stops working both when cases are already familiar (S013, S020) and when the learner's specific knowledge is too sparse to infer from (S020).

Same moderator as contradiction 3: feedback must be elaborated, the learner must have enough prior knowledge to use it, and there must be a reason to act. S018 fails on the second (very poor, error-prone prior knowledge, official-diagnosis feedback only) and on guidance (unguided task); S027 fails on the third (no credit points, so no revision).

Whether debiasing is embedded in practice or delivered as a warning, and whether the learner has the experience the technique assumes. Bias work succeeds when carried inside worked examples with elaborated feedback and annotated error records (S006, S023, S028). It fails as a warning: S024 reports learners still chose the common incorrect diagnosis despite an explicit availability-bias warning, and that novices lacking the experience to reason non-analytically fell back on feature-counting, which constrained the benefit.

Cognitive headroom. A reasoning prompt helps only when the learner has spare capacity to spend on it. S015's SBAR prompt mapped onto a structure the students already knew and reduced fear. The negatives are all headroom failures: underdeveloped illness scripts under demanding step-by-step comparison (S016), a typical presentation where the prompt is simply redundant (S019), and time pressure converting the prompt into frustration (S022).

Whether difficulty adapts to the learner. S011 and S015 succeed where pacing and scaffolding track the student. S022 fails because the challenge is fixed: timed case challenges triggered frustration in novice students, with the difficulty level reported as simply too high. The simulation is not the variable; its adjustability is.

Prior schema adequacy. Contrastive feature comparison pays when the learner already holds enough of a schema to hang the compared features on, and backfires when they do not: S016 reports that with underdeveloped illness scripts the same step-by-step comparison triggered high cognitive load, exhaustion and confusion, and S017 that feature tables applied to an UNTAUGHT murmur triggered incorrect feature identification that derailed reasoning. The comparison is not the active ingredient; having something to compare against is.

Instruction explicitness set against task difficulty. The coaching helps when it is explicit and the task outruns the learner's automatic pattern recognition. It adds nothing when the presentation is typical enough that heuristics already suffice (S019), turns harmful when the instruction itself is ambiguous (S021: a prompt 'whose meaning is not entirely clear' triggered confusion and LOWER accuracy), and fails when the strategy presupposes experience the learner lacks (S024).

The expertise gap between the model and the learner, and whether observation is active. Near-peer modelling works because it is cognitively congruent (S026, resident examples). Expert modelling fails for the same learners because experts skip and abstract steps the learner cannot reconstruct (S025). Independently, observation without active-processing prompts decays into passive listening and adds nothing on transfer (S025, S026 far-transfer without prompts).

Case familiarity, and it is an inverted U rather than a straight line. Self-explanation pays only where there is something to elaborate: it works on LESS familiar cases (S013, S020, S025, S026, all explicitly 'less familiar'), and produces no benefit once illness scripts are well defined and the case is familiar (S013; S020's familiar heart-failure cases show reduced engagement and elaboration). But it also fails at the other end, when specific knowledge is too thin to generate inferences from (S020). The window is 'unfamiliar enough to require reconstruction, familiar enough to permit it'.

Prompt specificity. A directive prompt aimed at a named object of thought works — S008's 'query your initial hypothesis' rectified incorrect diagnoses and, importantly, did no harm to correct ones. A free-choice prompt does not: S005 shows undergraduates left unguided with free-choice reasoning prompts self-selected a weaker strategy and scored BELOW the explicitly instructed group. For novices, directive beats permissive.

Prior familiarity with the structure being simulated, plus mandated versus optional use. S015 shows the SBAR prompt worked precisely for students ALREADY familiar with structured tools — reducing fear and increasing use — and that the same environment produced stress and abandonment where students had no prior multitasking experience. S011 adds the delivery condition: optional self-directed rollout produced limited uptake.

The feedback attached to the example, not the example. Both sides are S006. Worked examples carrying elaborated general-practitioner feedback lowered cognitive load and supported schema construction; the same erroneous examples carrying knowledge-of-correct-response feedback only — a bare right-or-wrong judgement — left learners with additive, mechanistic habits deducing from later cases instead. An example without an explanation is not a worked example.

Whether the reasoning strategy is explicitly taught or left to the learner. The clearest case in the set, because both sides come from ONE study with the same learners and the same ECGs: S004 participants 'instructed to reason in a combined manner' held their accuracy under misleading information, while those told to use 'whatever strategy comes naturally' lost accuracy when given an incorrect suggestion. The machine labelled both sides with identical contexts because they ARE identical on every dimension its taxonomy encodes; the instruction condition is not one of them.

Unstructured exposure only pays once a knowledge base exists. S009's positive case is a learner whose expertise was already developed through 'years of diligent study and practice'. Every negative case is exposure arriving before the prerequisite: no multitasking experience (S015), shadowing that leaves the student cocooned from decisions (S015), an untaught murmur (S017), novices without the experience non-analytic reasoning requires (S024). Apprenticeship is a multiplier on existing knowledge, not a substitute for it.

Learner readiness to exercise the control being handed over. S009's setting worked because it offered a discovery to someone equipped to recognise it. S005 shows free choice given to undergraduates with no prior ECG experience produced a worse strategy than being told what to do, and S019 that the control condition was already adequate for typical cases. Autonomy is an outcome of competence here, not a route to it.

Prior fluency with the medium, and whether the challenge can be adjusted. S022's positive finding is explicitly conditional on the population — 'many surgical clinicians ALREADY have video-game experience' — and produced enjoyment and voluntary replay. The same game under fixed timing frustrated novice medical students. S015 generalises it: a digital aid in an environment exceeding the learner's experience produces stress, not engagement.

Same moderator as contradiction 19, stated at mechanism level: worked-example support works through the elaborated explanation accompanying it. S006 against itself — elaborated feedback succeeds, knowledge-of-correct-response feedback alone does not.
